questions.question: What is a permission boundary in AWS IAM, and what does it do?
questions.answer: A permission boundary is an IAM advanced feature that sets the maximum permissions an identity-based policy can grant to a user or role. It never grants permissions by itself — it only caps what identity policies can give. Effective permissions are the intersection of the identity policy and the boundary. If the identity policy allows 10 actions and the boundary allows 3 of them, the user gets only those 3.

questions.question: What is the difference between a permission boundary and a session policy?
questions.answer: Both narrow permissions by intersection, but they differ in scope and duration. A permission boundary is a durable ceiling attached to an entity — it applies across all of that entity's sessions. A session policy is a per-call scope passed as a parameter to STS:AssumeRole — it applies only to that one assumption. Use a boundary for a standing cap; use a session policy for single-assumption scoping.

questions.question: What are the three steps AWS IAM uses to evaluate authorization decisions?
questions.answer: Step 1: Explicit Deny — if any evaluated policy contains an explicit deny for the action, the request is denied immediately and evaluation stops. Step 2: Explicit Allow — if an explicit allow exists and no deny overrides it, the request is allowed. Step 3: Implicit Deny — if neither an explicit deny nor allow applies, the request is denied by default. AWS is deny-by-default.

questions.question: What is the two-policy handshake required for cross-account role assumption?
questions.answer: Two things must both be true: (1) the calling principal in the source account must have STS:AssumeRole permission for the target role, and (2) the role in the destination account must have a trust policy that names the calling principal (or its account) as a trusted entity. Both are required — one without the other means the assumption fails.

questions.question: After a principal assumes a role cross-account, whose policies govern the session?
questions.answer: The session is governed by the assumed role's permission policy and the role's own permission boundary. The calling principal's identity policies and permission boundaries are completely dropped — they are not evaluated for the session. Once the role is assumed, AWS treats the session as a local same-account identity in the destination account.

questions.question: What is the Confused Deputy problem in AWS, and how do you prevent it?
questions.answer: The Confused Deputy problem occurs when a third-party service (like a SaaS vendor) is tricked into accessing one customer's resources while acting on behalf of a different customer. It's prevented using the External ID condition in the role's trust policy. The vendor generates a unique value per customer and passes it on every AssumeRole call. The customer requires that exact value in the trust policy — so the assumption fails for any mismatched identifier.

questions.question: What is the difference between aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent and aws:MultiFactorAuthAge?
questions.answer: MultiFactorAuthPresent is a boolean that is set at session start and remains true for the entire session lifetime — it doesn't change as time passes. MultiFactorAuthAge is a numeric value in seconds measuring how long ago MFA was performed — it increases as the session ages. Use MultiFactorAuthPresent for read-only operations where session-level MFA is sufficient. Use MultiFactorAuthAge with NumericLessThan (e.g., 900) for destructive operations to enforce fresh MFA and defend against session hijacking.

questions.question: What are the four MFA mechanisms AWS IAM supports, and which is most phishing-resistant?
questions.answer: The four mechanisms are: (1) Virtual MFA — a TOTP app (Google Authenticator, Authy) — fast and free, but not phishing-resistant. (2) Hardware MFA — a physical token device — no phone dependency, but hardware procurement required. (3) FIDO Security Key — hardware with public key cryptography (Google Titan, YubiKey) — phishing-resistant, domain-bound. (4) Passkey — device-bound or syncable credential — phishing-resistant, smooth UX. FIDO security keys and passkeys are the most phishing-resistant and recommended for privileged identities.

questions.question: What is the difference between identity-based and resource-based policies in AWS IAM?
questions.answer: Identity-based policies attach to IAM principals (users, groups, roles) and answer 'what can this identity do?' The Principal element is implicit. Resource-based policies attach to AWS resources (S3 bucket, KMS key, Lambda, etc.) and answer 'who can do what to this resource?' The Principal element must be explicit. Resource-based policies can grant cross-account access without role assumption, and they can enforce absolute denies that override any identity-based allow.

questions.question: Why can IAM groups not be principals in resource-based policies?
questions.answer: IAM groups are containers for permission management — they are not IAM identities themselves. A group has no ARN that can be used as a principal. When writing resource-based policies (like S3 bucket policies), you must reference the underlying users or roles directly, not the groups they belong to.

questions.question: A developer tells you their IAM policy grants S3:GetObject but they keep getting Access Denied. How do you troubleshoot this?
questions.answer: (Situation) A developer's S3:GetObject calls were failing with Access Denied despite an identity-based Allow. (Task) Identify the blocking deny. (Action) Applied the three-step IAM evaluation rule: checked for an explicit deny somewhere in the evaluated policies. Looked in: the bucket policy for a resource-based deny, any permission boundaries on the user or role, service control policies from AWS Organizations, and any session policy if assuming a role. Found an explicit deny in the bucket policy targeting the developer's role. (Result) Removed the incorrect deny statement, verified access was restored, and documented the root cause to prevent recurrence.

questions.question: A SaaS vendor needs to access each customer's S3 bucket using the customer's role. How do you prevent cross-customer data leakage?
questions.answer: (Situation) A SaaS vendor assumes customer-provided IAM roles to read S3 data. Risk: the vendor's platform could be tricked into accessing Customer A's data while serving Customer B. (Task) Implement Confused Deputy protection per-customer. (Action) Added an STS External ID condition to each customer's trust policy using a unique value the vendor generates and controls per customer. Configured the vendor's platform to pass each customer's unique External ID on every AssumeRole call. (Result) Even if a different customer's role ARN is somehow passed, the assumption fails because the External ID doesn't match — Confused Deputy is eliminated.

questions.question: A security engineer wants junior administrators to be able to attach policies to developer users but never grant permissions beyond an approved set. How is this implemented?
questions.answer: (Situation) Junior admins are creating policies for developers, but the security team needs a guaranteed cap. (Task) Implement delegated administration with a guaranteed ceiling. (Action) Attached a permission boundary to each developer IAM user listing only the approved actions on the approved services. Configured the delegation process so junior admins can attach identity-based policies freely. (Result) No matter how broad a policy a junior admin attaches, the boundary caps the developer's effective permissions to the approved set — and the security team doesn't need to review each attachment manually.

questions.question: An EC2 instance in Account B needs to run transcoding jobs on encrypted videos in S3 in Account A. Walk through the architecture.
questions.answer: (Situation) Cross-account access to KMS-encrypted S3 objects from an EC2 workload. (Task) Build the access pattern without long-lived credentials. (Action) In Account A: created an IAM role with a trust policy naming Account B, permission policy allowing S3:GetObject on the bucket and KMS:Decrypt on the KMS key, updated the KMS key policy to allow the role to perform KMS:Decrypt, enabled CloudTrail data events on the bucket. In Account B: created an instance profile for the EC2 instances with STS:AssumeRole permission on Account A's role. (Result) EC2 assumes the role via STS, receives temporary credentials, reads and decrypts the videos, and the session expires automatically. No access keys stored on instances.

questions.question: A session is hijacked after MFA sign-in. The attacker tries to delete production S3 objects. How does the architecture prevent this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Session hijacking after morning MFA sign-in. (Task) Prevent destructive actions in hijacked sessions. (Action) Applied aws:MultiFactorAuthAge with NumericLessThan: 900 as a condition on all delete policies. This means any delete operation requires MFA to have been performed within the last 15 minutes — a hijacked session will fail this condition as time passes. (Result) The attacker's session retains MultiFactorAuthPresent: true (session-level boolean), but MultiFactorAuthAge has grown beyond 900 seconds, blocking all destructive operations.

questions.question: A developer adds a permission boundary to a developer user to restrict them to read-only S3. The developer assumes a role with full S3 access. Does the boundary cap the role session?
questions.answer: (Situation) Boundary on user, not on role. (Task) Determine if user boundary follows into assumed role. (Action) Reviewed IAM evaluation mechanics for role assumption: user policies and user boundaries are dropped when assume role call succeeds. The session is governed only by the role's policies and the role's own boundary. (Result) The boundary on the user does NOT apply during the role session. The developer gets the role's full S3 access. Correct fix: put the boundary on the role itself, not the user.

questions.question: Why does a cross-account call to a KMS-encrypted S3 bucket require both the IAM role policy AND the KMS key policy to allow KMS:Decrypt?
questions.answer: (Situation) Cross-account decryption failing even though IAM role allows KMS:Decrypt. (Task) Explain two-pronged authorization. (Action) KMS uses independent two-pronged authorization: the IAM role's permission policy must allow KMS:Decrypt (identity-side grant), AND the KMS key's resource policy must allow the role to use the key (resource-side grant). This applies in same-account scenarios too — cross-account just makes it more visible because the resource policy must explicitly name the cross-account principal. (Result) Added KMS:Decrypt to the KMS key policy for the role's ARN — access restored.

questions.question: How would you architect least-privilege access for an analytics team that needs read-only access to production S3 data but must never be able to delete anything?
questions.answer: (Situation) Analytics team needs read access, must never delete. (Task) Enforce no-delete without relying on everyone's judgment. (Action) Created a DataAnalyst IAM role with an identity-based policy granting only S3:GetObject on the specific bucket/prefix. Added a resource-based bucket policy with an explicit deny for S3:DeleteObject on the DataAnalyst role — this guarantee holds even if someone accidentally adds delete to the identity policy later. Added aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 900 condition to enforce fresh MFA for every read. (Result) Read access works after MFA sign-in. Delete is impossible regardless of identity policy changes — explicit deny always wins.

questions.question: A KMS-encrypted S3 access fails with Access Denied. Walk through the four-step debug process.
questions.answer: In order: (1) Check the principal's IAM policy in the source account — does it have STS:AssumeRole for the role, and does the role policy include both S3:GetObject and KMS:Decrypt? (2) Check the role's trust policy in the destination account — does it name the calling principal? (3) Check the bucket policy in the destination account — is there any explicit deny that would override the allow? (4) Check the KMS key policy in the destination account — does it independently permit the role to perform KMS:Decrypt? The most common miss is Step 4: people fix the IAM role policy but forget the KMS key policy also needs to allow it.

questions.question: What happens to CloudTrail when a cross-account role is assumed and used?
questions.answer: (Situation) Audit trail for cross-account access. (Task) Understand where CloudTrail logs events. (Action) When EC2 in Account B assumes a role in Account A, the STS:AssumeRole call is logged in CloudTrail in Account B (source). All subsequent API calls made using the assumed role (S3:GetObject, KMS:Decrypt) are logged in Account A's CloudTrail under the assumed role's identity. If CloudTrail data events are enabled on the S3 bucket in Account A, every object read is captured there. (Result) Enabling CloudTrail data events on the source bucket in Account A is the compliance team's requirement — it provides an audit trail of every cross-account read.

questions.question: Design an IAM architecture that satisfies: data analysts can read S3 data, must never delete it, must use fresh MFA for every read, and developers getting temporary analyst access must not gain more than their normal dev permissions. Select two IAM controls.
questions.answer: Control 1: Attach an identity-based policy to the DataAnalystRole granting S3:GetObject on the specific bucket with condition aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 900. This satisfies the read-with-fresh-MFA requirement. Control 2: Attach a resource-based bucket policy with an explicit deny for S3:DeleteObject on the DataAnalystRole, and attach a permission boundary to each developer's IAM user limiting maximum permissions to development scope. The boundary ensures that when a developer assumes DataAnalystRole, their effective permissions cannot exceed dev-level — the boundary on the role serves the per-entity cap, satisfying the 'no permission extension' requirement. The explicit deny in the bucket policy satisfies the no-delete requirement regardless of identity policy changes.

questions.question: Explain the IAM security stack — four mechanisms with their roles — and when to use each.
questions.answer: Four mechanisms with distinct roles: (1) Identity-based policies — the floor. Grant baseline permissions to users, groups, roles. Add condition keys for contextual constraints. (2) Permission boundaries — the ceiling. Cap maximum effective permissions for an entity across all its sessions. Use when delegating policy creation to prevent over-grant. (3) Resource-based policies — the gate. Attach to resources for absolute denies that override any allow, and to enable cross-account access without role assumption. (4) Condition keys — contextual gates. Apply constraints based on request context: source IP, MFA presence, MFA age, time of day, request tags, region. The exam tests whether you can match each security requirement in a scenario to the correct mechanism — often the correct answer is a combination of two or three mechanisms.

questions.question: Explain the session policy vs permission boundary decision rule for per-assumption vs standing caps.
questions.answer: The decision is clean: Use a session policy when you need to scope one specific assumption at the moment you make it — per-call, temporary, and does not affect the role for other callers. Use a permission boundary when you need a durable, standing cap on an entity across everything it does — it applies to all sessions of that identity regardless of who calls it or what policy is attached. Critical distinction: a permission boundary cannot deliver per-assumption scoping (it's static per entity). A session policy cannot deliver a standing cap across callers (it applies to one call only). SaaS per-customer scoping → session policy. Delegated admin ceiling → permission boundary.

questions.question: Why is aws:SourceIp NOT a solution to the Confused Deputy problem in SaaS cross-account access?
questions.answer: aws:SourceIp restricts where the AssumeRole call can originate from (which IP range). But in a SaaS scenario, all customers' role assumptions come from the same vendor platform IP range. If Customer A and Customer B both have trust policies allowing the vendor's IP range, the vendor's platform could still accidentally assume Customer A's role while processing Customer B's request — both roles trust the same IP. Source IP solves 'who can call from where' but not 'which customer is this call for.' External ID solves the customer-identity confusion by requiring a per-customer unique value.

questions.question: A company has the following requirement: only data analysts may read S3, analysts must not delete under any circumstances, every read must require fresh MFA within 15 minutes, and developers with temporary analyst access must not gain permissions beyond their developer scope. Identify all four IAM controls needed.
questions.answer: Control 1 (who can read): Identity-based policy on DataAnalystRole — grants S3:GetObject only. Control 2 (fresh MFA for reads): Condition on the identity policy — aws:MultiFactorAuthAge with NumericLessThan: 900. Control 3 (no delete ever): Resource-based bucket policy with explicit deny for S3:DeleteObject on DataAnalystRole — explicit deny wins over any future identity policy changes. Control 4 (developer scope cap): Permission boundary on each developer's IAM user limiting maximum permissions to developer work scope — when a developer assumes DataAnalystRole, the boundary on the role (not the user) enforces the per-role ceiling. Note: boundary on the user does NOT follow into the assumed session; the boundary must be on the role to enforce per-assumption caps. The correct architecture uses identity policy + condition for read control, resource policy explicit deny for delete prevention, and permission boundary on the role for the scope guarantee.
